citation.title: A Note on Close Elections and Regression Analysis of the Party Incumbency Advantage

standing_assumptions:
The paper (Statistics, Politics, and Policy 2014; 5(1-2): 1–11; printed and PDF page numbers coincide) states two propositions about estimators computed from a data set of elections indexed by pairs $it$ (region $i$, election $t$). Everything below was read from the page images.
[Model (1), Section 3.1, p. 5] “We now prove that a variant of the RD estimator is exactly reproduced by an OLS regression that includes all $N$ elections. Consider a statistical model that would motivate the use of the OLS estimator: $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX_{ijt}+u_{i(t+1)},\qquad(1)$$ where $DV_{i(t+1)}$ represents a dependent variable of interest in the $t+1^{th}$ election in region $i$, $DemWin_{it}$ is an indicator variable for whether or not the Democratic party won the $t^{th}$ election in region $i$, and $X_{ijt}$ represents one of $J$ control variables associated with election $t$ in region $i$.”
[Setting of Proposition 1, p. 5] “We now prove that, under suitable conditions, ordinary least squares estimation of the model in equation (1) will exactly reproduce the RD estimate, even if the model in equation (1) is not correct. Let $k$ (the bandwidth) be a number between 0 and 1. Supposing that only the Democratic and Republican parties contest each election, a set of sufficient conditions for estimator equality follow:”. The forcing variable is defined inside Condition 1 (p. 5): “$DemVot_{it}$ is the difference between Democratic and Republican vote share in election $t$ in region $i$.” Conditions 1–3 (p. 5) and the definitions of $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6) are transcribed in full in P023-T11.
[Model (2), Section 3.2, p. 6] “We now consider OLS estimators of model (1) such that the control variables include a polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$. We will demonstrate that such estimators will tend to approximate $\hat\tau_{RD}$ in large samples. Consider the special case of the model (1), $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jDemVot_{it}^{j}+u_{i(t+1)}.\qquad(2)$$”
[Appendix B, p. 10] “Assume $$\mathrm{E}[DV\mid DemVot]=g(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot<0]+f(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$$ where $g()$ is continuous on $[-1,0)$ and $f()$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. Let $\alpha=\lim_{x\uparrow0}g(x)$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha$. Note that we have not assumed that $\beta$ has a causal interpretation.” Sampling, same page: “If the sample is drawn i.i.d. from a population $U$ with $\mathrm{Supp}(DemVot)\supseteq[-k,k]$, where $k>0$, then for large enough $N$, we have $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\beta$.”
Not printed, and needed by a formal statement (each is the reading the validators used): (a) $DemVot_{it}\in[-1,1]$, a difference of two vote shares on the proportion scale: Appendix B works on $[-1,1]$ and the constant 1 in $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ presupposes it. The Remark to Condition 3 and Section 4 give bandwidths in percentage points; 0.5 percentage points is $k=0.005$ (clarity note P023-N001). (b) Under the two-party supposition, $DemWin_{it}=1$ when $DemVot_{it}>0$ and $DemWin_{it}=0$ when $DemVot_{it}<0$. Section 3.1 states no convention for $DemVot_{it}=0$ (Appendix B writes $\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$); Proposition 1 does not depend on one, because $DemVot=0$ lies in the central bin. (c) The letter $J$ has three uses: the number of controls in (1); the value $2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ in Condition 2, the number of bin indicators; and the polynomial degree in (2). (d) $N$ is the number of pairs $it$ in the data, and $it\in U$ means that the pair $(i,t)$ belongs to the set $U$. (e) Nothing in Conditions 1–3 keeps a bin from being empty. The indicator of an empty bin is identically zero, so the OLS coefficient vector of (1) is then not unique, while the coefficient on $DemWin$ is the same in every least-squares solution; the factors $|\tilde U_j|^{-1}$ of Appendix A are to be read over non-empty bins only (clarity note P023-E006). (f) The definition of $\alpha$ presupposes that $g$ has a finite left limit at 0 (P023-A001, not confirmed as an error). (g) Both propositions concern the estimators $\hat\beta_{OLS}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ and $\hat\tau_{RD}$ as functions of the data, and $\beta$ of Appendix B is the jump of the conditional mean at 0; no potential-outcome model and no causal assumption is part of either statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (‘the resulting estimates rely solely on data from close elections’), and Section 3.2, last paragraph (‘will also only use information from close elections’), as printed; the witness is the validators’ construction (linear control) and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with a correctly specified linear control (validator's construction; not in the paper). Six elections with margins $x=(x_1,\dots,x_6)=(-\tfrac34,-\tfrac14,-\tfrac1{400},\tfrac1{400},\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$ (the values of $DemVot$) and $d_i=\mathrm{I}[x_i\ge0]$, so $d=(0,0,0,1,1,1)$ (the values of $DemWin$). Bandwidth $k=\tfrac1{200}$, so $U_b=\{i:-k<x_i\le k\}=\{3,4\}$ and Condition 1 holds. Outcomes $y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i$, that is $y=(\tfrac{37}{80},\tfrac{39}{80},\tfrac{3999}{8000},\tfrac{4801}{8000},\tfrac{49}{80},\tfrac{51}{80})$, and $y'$ equal to $y$ except $y'_6=y_6+\tfrac1{100}=\tfrac{259}{400}$. For an outcome vector $z$ write $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)$ for the coefficient on $d$ in the OLS regression of $z$ on $(\mathbf 1,d,x)$, which is regression (2) with $J=1$; $\hat\tau_{RD}(z)$ for the difference in means over $U_b$; and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(z)$ for the coefficient on $d$ in the regression of Condition 2 with $k=\tfrac1{200}$.
Claims. (i) The matrix with columns $(\mathbf 1,d,x)$ has rank 3. (ii) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac1{10}$; indeed $y$ satisfies (2) exactly with $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $\beta=\tfrac1{10}$, $\gamma_1=\tfrac1{20}$ and $u=0$. (iii) For every $z\in\mathbb R^6$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)=\sum_iw_iz_i$ with $w=\tfrac1{139202}(20299,\,-59901,\,-99600,\,99600,\,59901,\,-20299)$. (iv) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')=\tfrac{1371721}{13920200}$, so $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')-\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=-\tfrac{20299}{13920200}\ne0$, although $y'_i=y_i$ for every $i\in U_b$ (the two vectors differ only at the margin $\tfrac34$). (v) $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')=y_4-y_3=\tfrac{401}{4000}$. (vi) In Condition 2, $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil=200$ and the six observations lie in bins $25,75,100,100,125,175$ (bin 100 is $(-k,k]$); the coefficient on $d$ is the same in every least-squares solution and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')=\tfrac{401}{4000}$. (vii) Consequence: the coefficient of the exactly specified polynomial regression (2) is not a function of the outcomes of the elections in $U_b$, while $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and the coarsened $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ are.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) (p. 6) with $J=1$, and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$, “the OLS estimator of $\beta$ in (2)” (Proposition 2, p. 7); $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b\equiv\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$ (p. 6); Condition 2, $X_{ijt}=\mathrm{I}[2j-J-1<DemVot_{it}/k\le2j-J+1]$, $J=2\lceil\frac{1-k}{2k}\rceil$ (p. 5), with the reference bin $X_{i0t}=\mathrm{I}[-J-1\le DemVot_{it}/k\le-J+1]$ of Appendix A (p. 9). Formal reading of ‘rely solely on data from close elections’ and ‘only use information from close elections’ (the validators’; validated.json, P023-E001, natural_reading): with the margins held fixed, the estimate takes the same value on any two outcome vectors that agree on the elections in the close-election window $U_b$. Defined by the validator (P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1–2): the six-point design, the two outcome vectors, and the weights $w=r/(r^{\top}r)$ with $r$ the residual of $d$ on the columns $(\mathbf 1,x)$.
canonical_claim.note: Every number above was recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed and agrees with P023-E001/v1/artifact/exact_results.json (finite_linear) and check.out. In (vi) all bins but five are empty, so $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the coefficient on $d$ common to all least-squares solutions (standing assumption (e)); dropping the empty bins gives the same value. Both outcome vectors are possible realizations of one exactly specified model: with independent errors $U_i\in\{-\tfrac1{100},0,\tfrac1{100}\}$ of probabilities $\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14$ and $Y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i+U_i$, $y$ is the draw with all errors zero and $y'$ the draw with one positive error at $x=\tfrac34$ (derivation.md, section 4); that is context and not part of the target. All outcomes lie strictly between 0 and 1. The comparison does not say that the finite-window value $\tfrac{401}{4000}$ equals the jump $\tfrac1{10}$; it says that a distant change moves the polynomial coefficient and moves neither $\hat\tau_{RD}$ nor the coarsened coefficient. What a proof establishes: the statements on pp. 3 and 7 are false for a correctly specified linear control. It does not touch Proposition 1, the abstract, or the ‘may’ sentence on p. 8, which the coarsened estimator makes true. The second validator's independent artifact is P023-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph, and Section 3.2, last paragraph, as printed (the same statements as P023-T1); the witness is the validators’ construction with the degree-7 control of estimator (c) and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with a correctly specified degree-7 control (validator's construction; not in the paper). Sixteen elections with margins $x_i\in\{\pm\tfrac18,\pm\tfrac28,\dots,\pm\tfrac88\}$ in increasing order, $x=(-8,-7,\dots,-1,1,\dots,7,8)/8$, and $d_i=\mathrm{I}[x_i>0]$. Bandwidth $k=\tfrac15$, so $U_b=\{i:-\tfrac15<x_i\le\tfrac15\}=\{8,9\}$ (the margins $-\tfrac18$ and $\tfrac18$) and Condition 1 holds. Outcomes $y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i+\tfrac1{100}x_i^7$, and $y'$ equal to $y$ except at the margin 1: $y_{16}=\tfrac{33}{50}$, $y'_{16}=\tfrac{67}{100}$. $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)$ is the coefficient on $d$ in the OLS regression of $z$ on $(\mathbf 1,d,x,x^2,\dots,x^7)$, which is regression (2) with $J=7$; $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ are as in P023-T1 with $k=\tfrac15$.
Claims. (i) The $16\times9$ matrix with columns $(\mathbf 1,d,x,\dots,x^7)$ has rank 9. (ii) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac1{10}$; $y$ satisfies (2) exactly with $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $\beta=\tfrac1{10}$, $\gamma_1=\tfrac1{20}$, $\gamma_7=\tfrac1{100}$, the other $\gamma_j=0$, and $u=0$. (iii) For every $z\in\mathbb R^{16}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)=\sum_iw_iz_i$ with $w=\tfrac1{1607}(-175,\,725,\,-685,\,-643,\,554,\,1289,\,239,\,-2911,\,2911,\,-239,\,-1289,\,-554,\,643,\,685,\,-725,\,175)$; every weight is non-zero. (iv) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')=\tfrac{3249}{32140}$, so $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')-\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac{7}{6428}\ne0$, although $y'_i=y_i$ for every $i\in U_b$. (v) $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')=y_9-y_8=\tfrac{11796481}{104857600}$. (vi) In Condition 2, $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil=4$, the bins are $[-1,-\tfrac35]$, $(-\tfrac35,-\tfrac15]$, $(-\tfrac15,\tfrac15]$, $(\tfrac15,\tfrac35]$, $(\tfrac35,1]$, the observations lie in bins $(0,0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4)$, and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')=\tfrac{11796481}{104857600}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P023-T1, with regression (2) at $J=7$, the degree of estimator (c) of Section 4 (p. 7: “Estimator (c) includes a degree 7 polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$”). Defined by the validator (P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 3): the sixteen-point design, the two outcome vectors and the weights $w=r/(r^{\top}r)$ with $r$ the residual of $d$ on the columns $(\mathbf 1,x,\dots,x^7)$.
canonical_claim.note: Recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed; agrees with exact_results.json (finite_degree7) and check.out. The baseline is exactly of degree 7 with a non-zero seventh-degree coefficient, so no further polynomial term can improve its fit; the same two-realization remark as in P023-T1 applies (derivation.md, section 4). The window $k=\tfrac15$ is wide; it is a valid bandwidth under the paper's conditions and was chosen by the validator to keep the design simple, and P023-T1 uses the narrow window $k=\tfrac1{200}$. A Lean proof can avoid inverting a $9\times9$ matrix: it suffices to check that $w$ lies in the column space of $(\mathbf 1,d,x,\dots,x^7)$, is orthogonal to the eight polynomial columns and has $w^{\top}d=1$. All outcomes lie strictly between 0 and 1 ($\tfrac{11}{25}\le y_i\le\tfrac{67}{100}$).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (p. 3), and Section 3.2, last paragraph (p. 7), as repaired by Sol: sole reliance on close-election outcomes is reserved for the coarsened regression of Proposition 1; for polynomial controls, a common discontinuity target together with non-zero weights on distant outcomes
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3) and p. 7 (PDF p. 7); the ‘may’ sentence of Section 5, p. 8 (PDF p. 8), is kept
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P023-E001, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: “For the coarsened specification, full-sample OLS exactly reproduces the specified close-election RD estimate. Under a correctly specified polynomial conditional mean, the polynomial OLS coefficient estimates the same cutoff discontinuity as the limiting RD estimator, while outcomes outside the close-election window also enter its estimation. A shared cutoff target alone does not imply equal observation weights, sampling variance, or finite-sample bias. Its causal interpretation and scope require the appropriate assumptions.”
Mathematical content, written out (validator's derivation, P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1, 5, 6 and 7). Data: $N$ elections with margins $x_i\in[-1,1]$, indicators $d_i\in\{0,1\}$ with $d_i=1$ if $x_i>0$ and $d_i=0$ if $x_i<0$, and outcomes $y_i\in\mathbb R$; $k\in(0,1)$; $U_b=\{i:-k<x_i\le k\}$.
(a) [Coarsened regression: exact localization.] Suppose $U_b$ contains $n_1\ge1$ observations with $d_i=1$ and $n_0\ge1$ with $d_i=0$ (Condition 1 implies this). Let $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ be the coefficient on $d$ in a least-squares fit of $y$ on an intercept, $d$ and the bin indicators of Condition 2. Then $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the same in every least-squares solution, and $\hat\beta_{OLS}=\sum_iw^{c}_iy_i$ with $w^{c}_i=1/n_1$ for $i\in U_b$ with $d_i=1$, $w^{c}_i=-1/n_0$ for $i\in U_b$ with $d_i=0$, and $w^{c}_i=0$ for $i\notin U_b$. Hence $\hat\beta_{OLS}=\hat\tau_{RD}$, and two outcome vectors that agree on $U_b$ give the same $\hat\beta_{OLS}$.
(b) [Polynomial regression: the weights.] Fix $J\ge1$, let $Z$ be the $N\times(J+1)$ matrix with rows $(1,x_i,\dots,x_i^{J})$, and suppose $[Z,d]$ has full column rank $J+2$. Put $r=d-Z(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}d$. Then $Z^{\top}r=0$, $r^{\top}d=r^{\top}r>0$, and the OLS coefficient on $d$ in the regression (2) of $y$ on $[Z,d]$ is $\hat\beta_{OLS2}=r^{\top}y/r^{\top}r=\sum_iw_iy_i$ with $w_i=r_i/(r^{\top}r)$; moreover $\sum_iw_i=0$, $\sum_iw_ix_i^{j}=0$ for $j=1,\dots,J$, and $\sum_iw_id_i=1$. Changing one outcome $y_i$ by $\delta$, and no other, changes $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ by exactly $w_i\delta$.
(c) [Polynomial regression: no exact localization.] In (b), suppose also that at least one $d_i=1$ and at least one $d_i=0$. Then the number of distinct non-zero margin values $x_i$ with $w_i=0$ is at most $2J$ (at most $J$ negative and at most $J$ positive). Consequently, if more than $2J$ distinct non-zero margin values lie outside $(-k,k]$, there are an observation $i\notin U_b$ and outcome vectors $y,y'$ that differ only at $i$, so agree on $U_b$, with $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)\ne\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')$, while $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')$ and, under the hypothesis of (a), $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')$.
(d) [Common target under exact polynomial specification.] In (b), suppose the outcomes are random with $\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\alpha+\beta d_i+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jx_i^{j}$ for every $i$. Then $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\beta$. If, given the margins, the errors $u_i=y_i-\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]$ are uncorrelated with variances $\sigma_i^2$, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N)=\sum_iw_i^2\sigma_i^2$, to which every observation with $w_i\ne0$ and $\sigma_i^2>0$ contributes a positive amount, whether or not it lies in $U_b$.
(e) [Population illustration, uniform margins.] Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1,1]$, $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$, $p_J$ the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-p_J$ and $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$. Then $p_1(x)=\tfrac12+\tfrac34x$, $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$, $r_1(\tfrac9{10})/v_1=-\tfrac{14}5$ and $\mathrm E[r_1^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_1=\tfrac18$; and $p_7(x)=\tfrac12+(11025x-40425x^3+63063x^5-32175x^7)/4096$, $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$, $r_7(\tfrac9{10})/v_7=-\tfrac{20283449}{6125000}$ and $\mathrm E[r_7^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_7=\tfrac{572158921}{10276044800}$. If $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}D+\tfrac1{20}X$ (for $J=1$), respectively $\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}D+\tfrac1{20}X+\tfrac1{100}X^7$ (for $J=7$), then the population OLS coefficient on $D$, $\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$, equals $\tfrac1{10}$, and the population RD difference $\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ equals $\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac k{20}$, respectively $\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac k{20}+\tfrac{k^7}{400}$, which tends to $\tfrac1{10}$ as $k\to0$: one target, and a strictly positive share of the OLS influence variance on $|X|\ge\tfrac12$.
(f) [Accepted 19 October shared-consistency qualification.] For every fixed tolerance ε>0, P(|A_N-B_N|>ε) ≤ P(|A_N-β|>ε/2)+P(|B_N-β|>ε/2). Consequently, if the actual polynomial OLS and shrinking-window RD estimators are both consistent in probability for β, their difference tends to zero in probability. No independence between them is required. The two consistency statements are explicit hypotheses, not conclusions of exact specification alone.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: Conditions 1–3, $U_b$, $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ (pp. 5–6; transcribed in P023-T11); regression (2) and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ (pp. 6–7). The printed sentences being replaced are transcribed in P023-T10. Defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections 1 and 5): the finite-sample residual $r$ and weights $w$; the population projection $p_J$, residual $r_J$ and $v_J$; and the influence-variance share $\mathrm E[r_J^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_J$ (under an exactly specified mean with independent homoskedastic errors $U$ the influence function of the OLS coefficient is $r_J(X)U/v_J$).
canonical_claim.note: Part (a) is Proposition 1 (P023-T11) in weight form and should reuse it. Parts (b)–(d) are exact finite-sample linear algebra for every $J$; they are the formal content of ‘outcomes outside the close-election window also enter its estimation’ and of ‘estimates the same cutoff discontinuity’. In (c) the validator states the count for a design with distinct margins (derivation.md, section 6: ‘Apart from at most 2J distinct margins, residuals and hence outcome weights are nonzero’); counting distinct non-zero margin values, as here, is the same argument and also covers repeated margins and a tie at 0. The argument: the fitted polynomial $p_J$ with coefficients $(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}d$ is neither the zero polynomial nor the constant 1, because its fitted values sum to $\sum_id_i\in[1,N-1]$; so $p_J$ vanishes at no more than $J$ negative margins and $p_J-1$ at no more than $J$ positive margins. Part (e) was recomputed exactly when this list was fixed (exact_results.json, population_degree1 and population_degree7). ‘The limiting RD estimator’ in the corrected text refers to consistency of $\hat\tau_{RD}$ for the jump as $k\to0$ and $Nk\to\infty$, which is part of P023-T8 and is not repeated here; a common target under merely approximate specification is the subject of P023-E002 (P023-T7, P023-T8). The last two sentences of the corrected text are a non-implication and a caution about interpretation: their formal content is that the weights of (a) and of (b) differ in designs where both estimators have the same target (P023-T1, P023-T2 and (e)). No claim is made that two estimators with one target differ in causal scope or in external validity. The artifact's comparison of leading noise variances ($16\sigma^2/N$ and $(65536/1225)\sigma^2/N$ against $4\sigma^2/(Nk)$) is a leading-order remark and is not a target. The accepted review's shared-consistency implication is now formalized separately in P023_Review.polynomial_rd_shared_consistency, using the actual estimator definitions and a finite ε/2 union bound. This does not finish the broader regularity theorem T8.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Remark to Proposition 2 (‘we require that the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms’), read with Appendix B (‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’), as printed; the witness (uniform margins, degrees 1 and 7) is the settling validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with one fixed, regular margin distribution (settling validator's construction; not in the paper). Let $X$ ($=DemVot$) be uniform on $[-1,1]$ and $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ ($=DemWin$). For $a>0$ and $0<\eta\le1$ let $h_\eta(x)=a\cdot\mathrm{clip}(x/\eta,-1,1)$, that is $h_\eta(x)=ax/\eta$ for $|x|\le\eta$ and $a\,\mathrm{sign}(x)$ otherwise, and $Y=\tfrac12+h_\eta(X)+U$ with $U=\pm\tfrac1{10}$ equiprobable and independent of $X$. For $J\ge1$ let $q_J$ be the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-q_J$, $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$, and $b_J=\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$, the population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ (the probability limit of $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ at fixed $J$).
Claims. (i) $h_\eta$ is continuous, odd and $(a/\eta)$-Lipschitz with $h_\eta(0)=0$, and $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+h_\eta(X)$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$; so Appendix B's assumptions hold with $g$ and $f$ the restrictions of $\tfrac12+h_\eta$, $\alpha=\tfrac12$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha=0$. (ii) The population RD difference $\tau_k=\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ equals $ak/\eta$ for $0<k\le\eta$, so $\tau_k\to0=\beta$ as $k\to0$. (iii) $r_1(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac34x$ for $x>0$ and $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$; $r_7(x)=\tfrac12-(11025x-40425x^3+63063x^5-32175x^7)/4096$ for $x>0$ and $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$; $r_J(-x)=-r_J(x)$ for $x\ne0$. (iv) $b_J-\beta=2a-\dfrac a{v_J}\displaystyle\int_0^{\eta}r_J(x)\Big(1-\frac x\eta\Big)dx$. Hence $b_1=2a(1-\eta)^2$, and for $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $b_7=\tfrac1{10}-\tfrac{4096}{6125}\eta+\tfrac65\eta^2-\tfrac{33}{25}\eta^4+\tfrac{858}{875}\eta^6-\tfrac{143}{490}\eta^8$. At $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $\eta=\tfrac1{10000}$: $b_1=\tfrac{99980001}{1000000000}$ and $b_7=\tfrac{4896723787999993532000048047999857}{49000000000000000000000000000000000}$, that is 9.998 and 9.993 percentage points of vote share, with $\beta=0$ and $Y\in[\tfrac7{20},\tfrac{13}{20}]$. (v) [Fit.] The predictor $\tfrac12+a(2D-1)$ lies in the span of $(1,D)$, hence of the regressors of (2) at every degree, and $\mathrm E[(h_\eta(X)-a(2D-1))^2]=a^2\eta/3$. So the population mean squared error of the fitted regression (2), at any degree, exceeds the irreducible $\mathrm E[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]=\tfrac1{100}$ by at most $a^2\eta/3$, and no additional function of $X$, polynomial or not, can lower it by more than $a^2\eta/3$; at $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $\eta=\tfrac1{10000}$ this is $\tfrac1{12000000}$, at most $\tfrac1{120000}$ of the current mean squared error. (vi) For fixed $J$ and $a$, $b_J\to2a$ as $\eta\downarrow0$, while the bound in (v) tends to 0.
Consequence: with uniform margins and a Lipschitz smooth part, the fit of a linear or a degree-7 control ‘cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms’, yet for $J=1$ and for $J=7$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\to_pb_J\approx0.1$ while $\hat\tau_{RD}\to_p\beta=0$ as $N\to\infty$, $k\to0$, $Nk\to\infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) (p. 6) and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ (p. 7); Appendix B's $g$, $f$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $h$ (p. 10; transcribed in P023-T12); $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6). The Remark (p. 7): “Put simply, in order for the result to hold, we require that the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms in the polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$.” Defined by the validators and not in the paper: the population projection $q_J$, residual $r_J$, $v_J$ and coefficient $b_J$; for fixed $J$ and an i.i.d. sample with $\mathrm E[Y^2]<\infty$ and a positive definite moment matrix, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\to_pb_J$ (P023-T8(d)). Formal reading of the fit criterion (the settling validator's; P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, section 2, equation (4)): the supremum of the reduction in population mean squared error obtainable by adding further terms to the fitted regression.
canonical_claim.note: Source: derivation.md, section 7, equations (20)–(22), with check_exact.py and exact_results.json (sigmoid_example, sigmoid_bias_family_eta). The closed forms for $b_1$ and $b_7$, both rational values and the bound $\tfrac1{12000000}$ were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed. This is the example the rating of P023-E002 cites (‘uniform margins, zero jump, a degree-1 or degree-7 coefficient about 10 points off with a further gain in fit below 1/12,000,000’). It refutes the Remark's criterion read as sufficient, and Appendix B's step from a small error in the fitted conditional mean to a small error in the coefficient; it does not refute Proposition 2 for a sufficiently large degree, because $h_\eta$ is Lipschitz and P023-T8 applies to it. A caution for the reader of the example: the smooth part rises by $2a$ within $(-\eta,\eta)$, so at a fixed bandwidth $k>\eta$ the difference in means is $\tau_k=2a-a\eta/k$, close to $2a$; the statement concerns the limit $k\to0$ of Proposition 2, in which $\tau_k=ak/\eta\to0$. The noise $U$ affects neither $b_J$ nor $\tau_k$; it fixes the irreducible error used in (v). The polynomial error of $h_\eta$ itself is not small ($\inf_p\sup|h_\eta-p|$ is of order $a$): the example separates ‘further gain in fit of the fitted regression’ from ‘polynomial approximation error of $h$’, which P023-T7 bounds.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix B, the step ‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’, as printed; the witness (a margin distribution concentrated near $\pm\tfrac12$, linear control) is the validators' construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 10 (PDF p. 10); Proposition 2 and its Remark, p. 7 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness that a uniformly small error in the polynomial approximation of the conditional mean does not bound the error in the coefficient (validator's construction; not in the paper). Fix $a=\tfrac12$, $d=\tfrac1{1000}$, $w=d/2=\tfrac1{2000}$, $q=d^4=10^{-12}$. Let $t_{c,w}(x)=\max(w-|x-c|,0)/w^2$ and let $X$ ($=DemVot$) have the density $\rho(x)=\tfrac q2+\tfrac{1-q}2\{t_{a,w}(x)+t_{-a,w}(x)\}$ on $[-1,1]$; $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$. Let $h$ be odd with, for $x\ge0$: $h(x)=0$ for $x\notin[a-2w,a+2w]$; $h(x)=a-2w-x$ on $[a-2w,a-w]$; $h(x)=x-a$ on $[a-w,a+w]$; $h(x)=a+2w-x$ on $[a+w,a+2w]$. Let $Y=\tfrac12+h(X)+U$ with $U=\pm\tfrac1{10}$ equiprobable and independent of $X$.
Claims. (i) $\rho$ is a continuous probability density on $[-1,1]$ with $\rho\ge q/2>0$ (full support, positive and continuous at 0, no atom). $h$ is continuous, odd and 1-Lipschitz, vanishes on $[-(a-2w),a-2w]$, and $\sup|h|=w=\tfrac1{2000}$. So Appendix B's assumptions hold with $g$, $f$ the restrictions of $\tfrac12+h$, $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $\beta=f(0)-\alpha=0$; and $Y\in[\tfrac{799}{2000},\tfrac{1201}{2000}]$. (ii) With $\gamma_1=\dots=\gamma_J=0$, $|h(x)-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jx^j|\le\tfrac1{2000}$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ and every $J$. (iii) $\mathrm E[X]=\mathrm E[h(X)]=0$, $\mathrm E[(D-\tfrac12)h(X)]=0$, $\mathrm E[XD]=\tfrac14$, $\mathrm E[X^2]=(1-q)(a^2+\tfrac{w^2}6)+\tfrac q3$ and $\mathrm E[Xh(X)]=(1-q)\tfrac{w^2}6+2qw^3$. (iv) The population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X)$, regression (2) with $J=1$, is $$b_1=-\frac{(1-q)w^2/6+2qw^3}{(1-q)w^2/6+q/12}=-\frac{499999999999503}{500000999999500}\approx-0.999998,$$ against $\beta=0$. (v) For every $0<k<a-2w=\tfrac{499}{1000}$ the population RD difference $\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ is 0. (vi) $\mathrm E[h(X)^2]\le w^2=\tfrac1{4000000}$, so no predictor of $Y$ from $X$ improves on the population mean squared error of the constant $\tfrac12$ by more than $\tfrac1{4000000}$ (the irreducible error is $\tfrac1{100}$). (vii) [Family.] For $0<d\le\tfrac12$, with $a=\tfrac12$, $w=d/2$ and $q=d^4$, $b_1(d)=-\dfrac{1-d^4+6d^5}{1-d^4+2d^2}\to-1$ as $d\downarrow0$, while $\sup|h|=d/2\to0$ and $\beta=0$.
Consequence: at $J=1$ there is no constant $C$, free of the law of $DemVot$, with $|b_1-\beta|\le C\sup_x|h(x)-\gamma_1x|$ for all such laws and all $\gamma_1$; continuity, full support and a positive density at 0 do not give ‘$\mathrm E[u\mid DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ (pp. 6–7); Appendix B's $g$, $f$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, $h$ and its step from the uniform approximation to the coefficient (p. 10; transcribed in P023-T12). Defined by the validator (P023-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2–3): the density $\rho$, the function $h$, the noise $U$, and the population coefficient $b_1$, obtained from the normal equations of $Y-\tfrac12$ on $(D-\tfrac12,X)$, which by symmetry are $\begin{pmatrix}1/4&1/4\\1/4&\mathrm E[X^2]\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\c_1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\mathrm E[Xh(X)]\end{pmatrix}$.
canonical_claim.note: This is the exact example recorded in Sol's verdict (validated.json, P023-E002, what_is_established: ‘victory coefficient -499999999999503/500000999999500 at J=1’). The moments in (iii), the value in (iv), $\mathrm E[h(X)^2]=\tfrac{249999999999751}{6000000000000000000000}$ and the closed form in (vii) were recomputed by exact integration when this list was fixed. The artifact also certifies a degree-7 instance with $q=d^{32}$: $-\tfrac{1001}{1000}<b_7<-\tfrac{999}{1000}$ (derivation.md, section 4; exact_results.json); it involves rationals of about a thousand digits and is not part of this target. The second validator's variant uses uniform instead of triangular windows and obtains $b_1=-\tfrac{999999999999003}{1000000999999000}$ (P023-E002/v2/artifact/derivation.md). Scope, as the validators state it: each member of the family is a different law, so this is not a counterexample to Proposition 2 for one fixed law as $J\to\infty$; each member has a density bounded below and a 1-Lipschitz $h$, so P023-T8 applies to it and $b_J\to\beta$ for $J$ large enough, far beyond 1 or 7. The fixed-law failure under continuity alone is P023-T6, and the fixed-law failure of the fit criterion is P023-T4.
